title: The unfinished Jagannath
hook: a god left without hands or feet, and the rite that makes an image a home
carry: prana pratishtha: the presence is invited, not bought
tomorrow: Sam says chakras are fake. is he right, or asking the wrong question?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pusalar's temple built in the mind, and manasa puja: worship offered in the mind is real worship. Today, back to wood and brass, and a god who was never finished.

In the best-known telling, King Indradyumna longs for an image of Vishnu for his temple at Puri. A log of sacred wood washes in from the sea, and an old carpenter offers to carve it, on one condition: twenty-one days behind closed doors, and no one looks. Days pass. Then the sound of the chisel stops. The queen fears the old man has died, and the doors are opened early. The carpenter is gone. The images stand unfinished: great round eyes, no hands, no feet.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE DAYS, DOORS SHUT.` → `THE CHISEL STOPS.` → `NO HANDS, NO FEET.`

segments.voice: The king is heartbroken. But in the story he's told to install them just as they are. And that's how Jagannath, Lord of the World, has been worshipped at Puri ever since, with his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra: round-eyed, unfinished, loved by millions. The Purana's telling even sends the king to Brahma, the creator, to consecrate the temple. So what made rough wood a god? Hindu worship has a rite for exactly this, called prana pratishtha. Prana is breath, life; pratishtha is establishing. Before an image or a yantra is worshipped as a home of the divine, the rite invites the presence in. After it, the image is greeted, bathed, offered flowers and a lamp, morning after morning. Details differ by lineage and teacher, but the teaching is plain: holiness isn't in the material or the finish. It's invited, then cared for. Puri shows it boldly. Every so often, in a year the calendar marks for it, new images are carved from fresh neem wood, and in a secret night rite the sacred core of the old ones is moved into the new. The old wood is buried. The god goes on. Now picture a brass Sri Yantra in a shop near a temple, a price sticker on one corner, and the same lines on a home altar under fresh flowers. One has been installed and cared for. The other hasn't, though to people who honor the Goddess its lines still point to her, so handle it with care.
screen: `INSTALL THEM AS THEY ARE.` · `PRANA PRATISHTHA: INVITING THE PRESENCE.` · `INSTALLED, THEN CARED FOR.` · `NEW WOOD, THE SAME GOD.` · then, large: `INVITED, NOT BOUGHT.`

segments.voice: If there's a shrine or an image at home, stand before it for the sit and greet it the way families do each morning, with folded hands and a quiet name. If not, rest your eyes on one object that matters more than it cost, and notice that what made it precious was never the material.
The Sri Yantra: the same lines in a shop or on an altar. Prana pratishtha and daily worship make one of them a home of the Goddess.
Something to hold: prana pratishtha. The presence is invited, not bought, as in Jagannath's unfinished wood. Day sixteen-forty, done.

howItsDone: Before a Sri Yantra or an image is worshipped, it is usually installed with the rite of prana pratishtha; afterward it is honored with flowers, a lamp and kumkum. Details differ by lineage and teacher. At Puri, the wooden images of Jagannath are periodically renewed in the Nabakalebara rite.
